questionText: How do you choose the right collection for a job? Give a decision guide.
shortAnswer: Order the questions: concurrency? ordering? uniqueness? indexed access? mutation pattern? growth? The answers select among List, HashSet, Dictionary, Queue/Stack, Sorted variants, concurrent types, or immutable/frozen — with arrays/spans for buffers.
detailedAnswer: Walk the tree: (1) Multiple threads? → Concurrent* or Channel (or lock + plain type for low contention). (2) Need ordering? Sorted* for maintained order, PriorityQueue for min/max only, List for insertion order. (3) Uniqueness? HashSet (+ comparer) or Dictionary for keyed. (4) Keyed lookup? Dictionary (frozen if static). (5) Random access by index? List/array. (6) FIFO/LIFO? Queue/Stack. (7) Append-only scan? List or array (cache wins). (8) Frequent middle edits? LinkedList (with node handles) or rethink the algorithm. (9) Shared snapshots? Immutable*/frozen. (10) Buffers? ArrayPool/Span. Then size the choice: known counts → capacity; static data → freeze; hot membership → HashSet; hot mapping → Dictionary with right comparer. Document the decision in a comment when non-obvious (// HashSet: O(1) membership for 200k SKUs). Revisit when profiles disagree — the guide picks the starting point, measurements pick the winner. Anti-guide: defaulting to List<T> for everything (queues, sets, maps disguised as lists are the top accidental-quadratics).
internalWorking: No single structure dominates: arrays win scans (prefetch), hashes win probes (O(1)), trees win ordered ops (O(log n)), and lock-free designs win contention. The guide maps workload shape to the structure whose strengths align — constants and comparers decide ties.
realWorldUsage: Design reviews (justify the collection in one line), refactoring accidental-O(n²) loops, and onboarding checklists for data-heavy services.
commonMistake: List<T> as universal hammer, Dictionary for two-element maps (overhead + comparer ceremony — use switch/tuple), and Sorted* without an ordering requirement (log-factor tax for nothing).
technicalConversation: Ask them to defend their last collection choice against two alternatives — the complexity + comparer + concurrency vocabulary is the maturity signal.
interviewFollowUp: When would you deliberately pick a 'slower' structure, and what would you measure to confirm?
keyTakeaway: Concurrency → concurrent, order → sorted, membership → set, lookup → map, scan → list/array. Decide, document, measure.

questionText: How do you safely iterate and mutate shared collections across threads?
shortAnswer: Never mutate a plain collection during cross-thread enumeration. Snapshot (ToArray) for readers, lock mutations, or use concurrent collections (snapshot enumeration) / channels (handoff) / immutable swaps (Interlocked.Exchange) depending on read/write ratios.
detailedAnswer: The failure modes: version exceptions (same-thread mutation), torn reads (cross-thread without sync — no exception, just wrong data), and lock convoys (coarse lock under read-heavy load). Patterns by ratio: (1) Read-heavy, rare writes → immutable swap: private ImmutableDictionary field, writers Interlocked.Exchange a rebuilt copy, readers never lock (config tables, route maps). (2) Balanced → ConcurrentDictionary/ConcurrentQueue with snapshot enumeration (ToArray for stable views). (3) Handoff, not sharing → Channel<T> (ownership transfers, no shared state at all — the best answer when it fits). (4) Legacy/low contention → lock + ToList snapshot inside the lock, enumerate outside (keeps the lock tiny). ReaderWriterLockSlim for read-dominant with occasional writes (recursion pitfalls — avoid upgrades). Never: lock-free DIY on plain collections, volatile as a substitute for locking, or ConcurrentBag.Count-based logic. Testing: stress with Parallel + ThreadStress (TSAN-style race plug-ins are thin on .NET — rely on stress + code review), and assert invariants (counts, no duplicates) rather than exact interleavings.
internalWorking: Immutable swap publishes atomically (reference write) with safe publication via Interlocked (full fence); old versions stay alive for in-flight readers (GC reclaims). Concurrent enumeration walks segments with version tolerance (may include recently-added, never corrupt). lock uses Monitor thin-lock (spin then kernel wait).
realWorldUsage: Route/handler registries, feature-flag tables, connection maps, metrics registries, and plugin catalogs reloaded at runtime.
commonMistake: ToList outside the lock (torn snapshot), lock per element (convoy + deadlock ordering), ConcurrentDictionary iteration assumed fresh (it is a snapshot — document staleness tolerance), and forgetting Complete/stop signals for handoff loops.
technicalConversation: Ask what 'safe' means for their readers — exactness (lock+snapshot), freshness (concurrent), or consistency (immutable swap)? Different answers, different tools.
interviewFollowUp: Why is a torn read worse than an exception, and how do you test for something that fails silently?
keyTakeaway: Share nothing (channels), swap immutably (reads), snapshot under lock (legacy). Torn reads fail silently — design them away.

questionText: What production bugs do custom equality comparers cause, and how do you prevent them?
shortAnswer: Hash/equals disagreement (silent lookup misses), mutable fields in GetHashCode (vanishing entries), culture-sensitive hashing (Turkish-I), and case drift between writers/readers. Prevent with: hash==equals contract tests, immutable key fields, explicit StringComparer, and comparer unit tests with adversarial inputs.
detailedAnswer: The hall of fame: (1) GetHashCode includes a mutable field (Status) — entries vanish after status changes; fix: hash immutable identity only. (2) Equals compares case-insensitively but GetHashCode is case-sensitive — 'User' and 'user' land in different buckets yet compare equal → duplicates + misses; fix: derive both from the same normalized form. (3) CurrentCulture in hashing — Turkish 'I' vs 'ı' splits keys by machine locale; fix: Ordinal/OrdinalIgnoreCase everywhere for technical keys. (4) Record with collection property as key — reference equality on the list breaks value semantics; fix: key on a computed stable string or exclude collections. (5) NaN/negative-zero edge in double keys (NaN != NaN — Dictionary handles via special-casing, custom code often doesn't). Defenses: contract test per comparer (equal ⇒ same hash; unequal ⇒ usually different; transitivity trio), fuzz with cultures (test under tr-TR), seal key types, and prefer BCL comparers (StringComparer.Ordinal*) over hand-rolled. Debugging: missing-key incidents where the key 'is right there' — dump bucket index vs computed hash to confirm placement corruption.
internalWorking: Placement = hash % buckets; lookup walks only that chain. Disagreement means equal keys live in different chains — Equals never runs across chains, so misses are silent (no exception, just wrong answers). Culture-sensitive hashing folds differently per locale (i/I mappings), splitting keys across machines.
realWorldUsage: Dedup pipelines, idempotency-key maps, username/email indexes, cache keys, and test comparers — anywhere custom equality meets production data.
commonMistake: Mutable hash fields, culture-aware technical keys, record-collection keys, and NaN double keys in hand-rolled structures.
technicalConversation: Ask how they would test a new comparer — equal/hash/transitivity trio plus Turkish-locale and case-variant fuzz is the senior answer.
interviewFollowUp: Why do silent misses make comparer bugs harder to find than crashes, and what telemetry would catch them?
keyTakeaway: Hash must agree with equals, over immutable ordinal-normalized data. Contract-test every comparer.

questionText: How do you diagnose a memory leak caused by ever-growing collections?
shortAnswer: Confirm Gen2 growth + find the root chain (who holds the list) via dotnet-gcdump/dump analysis. Classic culprits: static caches without eviction, event subscriptions pinning graphs, un unbounded queues, and forgotten timers. Fix with bounds, eviction (LRU/MemoryCache), weak references, or unsubscribe discipline.
detailedAnswer: Process: (1) Confirm: memory climbs monotonically under steady load (not sawtooth) — Gen2 + LOH growth in counters; task-manager MB alone proves nothing. (2) Capture: dotnet-gcdump (lightweight) or full dump (dotnet-dump collect) at two points in time; diff object counts — the growing type is the leak. (3) Root: !gcroot (SOS) or the gcdump reference view — follow the chain to the static/event/cache holder. Top offenders: static List/Dictionary caches with no cap (add SizeLimit/eviction), events on long-lived publishers (each subscriber graph leaks — unsubscribe or weak events), BlockingCollection/Channel producers without bounds (backpressure instead), HttpClient/DbContext-looking statics holding response buffers, and ConditionalWeakTable misused as a cache (it never evicts by design). Fixes: MemoryCache with SizeLimit + expiration, LRU hand-rolled only with proven need, WeakReference for non-owning links (resurrection pitfalls — keep short), and Dispose patterns that unsubscribe. Prevention: cache review checklist (bound? expiry? metrics?), roslyn analyzers for undisposed subscriptions in UI code, and load tests asserting flat memory.
internalWorking: Leaked graphs survive to Gen2 (expensive, rarely collected) and pin LOH if large. gcdump walks the heap recording types + references; diffing two dumps isolates growth. SOS !gcroot traces reference chains to roots (statics, handles, stacks). Event leaks root through the publisher's delegate invocation list (_target chains).
realWorldUsage: Long-running APIs/workers, desktop apps with view-model leaks, caches, subscription hubs (SignalR connection maps), and batch processors accumulating results.
commonMistake: Calling it a leak from task-manager numbers (could be normal Gen2/LOH behavior), restarting instead of rooting (the leak returns), WeakReference as a cache (no eviction policy — use real caches), and event += without -= on short-lived subscribers.
technicalConversation: Ask for their last memory incident's root chain — static → cache → entries → payloads is the classic shape; the follow-up is what bound/expiry they added.
interviewFollowUp: Why do event subscriptions leak the subscriber and not the publisher, and what breaks that chain?
keyTakeaway: Confirm Gen2 growth, diff dumps, follow gcroot to the holder. Bound + expire every cache; unsubscribe every event.

questionText: How do you page, stream, or chunk large in-memory datasets without blowing memory?
shortAnswer: Never ToList() unbounded data. Page at the source (keyset/Skip-Take), stream with yield/IAsyncEnumerable, or chunk into fixed batches (Chunk()) for processing. Each keeps the working set flat regardless of total size.
detailedAnswer: Options by source: (1) Database: keyset pagination (WHERE id > last ORDER BY id LIMIT n — stable under inserts, unlike offset which skips/duplicates on shifting data) or Skip/Take with order for small sets. (2) In-memory enumerable: .Chunk(size) (.NET 6+) for fixed batches — export, bulk insert, parallel fan-out per chunk. (3) Async streams: await foreach over IAsyncEnumerable with cancellation — constant memory for files/sockets/APIs. (4) Channels: producer streams chunks, N consumers process (bounded → backpressure included). UI: virtualize (WPF VirtualizingStackPanel, web grid paging) — render windows, not datasets. API design: cursor/opaque-token paging over page numbers (stable + unguessable). Sizes: 100–1000 rows per page for APIs (latency vs round-trips), 1k–10k for bulk DB ops (parameter limits, transaction size), chunk bytes (~80KB to stay sub-LOH). Anti-patterns: ToList then .Take (materializes everything to discard most), Skip without OrderBy (nondeterministic pages), and offset paging deep into millions (O(offset) scan per page — keyset instead).
internalWorking: Chunk buffers one batch array at a time (prior batches GC-eligible). Keyset uses the clustered index seek (no scan). Offset (Skip) still reads+discards offset rows per page — cost grows with page number. IAsyncEnumerable streams with compiler state machines (no buffering).
realWorldUsage: Export endpoints, ETL batches, admin grids, search indexing, bulk email sends, and migration backfills.
commonMistake: Unbounded ToList (the LOH bomb), offset deep-paging (linear slowdown per page), Skip without OrderBy (shifting pages), and page-number APIs for unguessable data (use cursors).
technicalConversation: Ask what their biggest endpoint returns today — unbounded lists are the incident class; keyset + Chunk is the remediation vocabulary.
interviewFollowUp: Why does keyset pagination stay stable when rows insert mid-walk, while offset does not?
keyTakeaway: Page at the source, chunk in memory, stream async flows. Working set flat, total size irrelevant.

questionText: How do you build a correct expiring cache with MemoryCache, and what are its limits?
shortAnswer: MemoryCache with SizeLimit + absolute/sliding expiration + eviction callbacks covers most bounded caches. Limits: per-process (no distribution), approximate size accounting, and no LRU guarantee — for distributed/shared needs use IDistributedCache (Redis), for strict LRU hand-roll dictionary+linked-list.
detailedAnswer: Setup: new MemoryCache(new MemoryCacheOptions { SizeLimit = 1024, CompactionPercentage = 0.25, TrackStatistics = true }) — SizeLimit is mandatory for eviction to engage (entries need Size set). Policies per entry: AbsoluteExpiration(RelativeToNow) for freshness guarantees, SlidingExpiration for idle eviction, PostEvictionCallbacks for logging/reload, NeverRemove priority for pinned entries, and CancellationChangeToken/dependencies for external invalidation. GetOrCreate(_Async) for stampede-safe loads (factory runs once per key — with its own caveats under races; Lazy<Task<T>> inside for true once-only async). Statistics (GetCurrentStatistics) feed hit-rate dashboards — the only cache metric that matters. Limits: in-process only (each replica caches separately — stampedes multiply; use IDistributedCache/Redis + local L1 for shared), size is whatever you declare (measure payloads — a 'size 1 per entry' lie with 1MB values still OOMs), compaction is approximate LRU (not strict), and expiration scans are periodic (stale reads between scans are normal). Alternatives: hand-rolled LRU (strict order, custom accounting), ConcurrentDictionary + timers (DIY expiry bugs), and CDN/DB caching layers above/below.
internalWorking: Entries live in a ConcurrentDictionary with manual size summation; expiration scans on a timer + access; over-limit triggers compaction (removes lowest-priority ~percentage). GetOrCreate uses per-key locks to serialize factory runs (async variant holds no lock across awaits — uses task caching; concurrent factory runs possible without Lazy<Task>).
realWorldUsage: Reference data, rendered fragments, auth-session state, rate-limit buckets, and downstream-response memoization.
commonMistake: No SizeLimit (unbounded = leak), Size lies (OOM despite 'limits'), per-entry timers (use policy expirations), caching per-request data (no reuse — pure overhead), and ignoring stampedes (thundering herd on expiry — Lazy<Task> or GetOrCreate).
technicalConversation: Ask for their cache hit rate — no metric means no cache discipline; 90%+ with bounded size and expirations is the healthy shape.
interviewFollowUp: Why is MemoryCache compaction only approximate LRU, and when does that matter?
keyTakeaway: SizeLimit + expirations + callbacks + hit-rate metrics. In-process only; distributed needs Redis.

questionText: How do you batch database writes from an in-memory queue without losing data?
shortAnswer: Buffer into bounded batches (count or time window, whichever hits first), write transactionally per batch, acknowledge/remove only after commit, and persist-or-replay on crash (outbox table or durable queue) when loss is unacceptable.
detailedAnswer: The pattern: producers enqueue events; a flusher drains up to N or every T ms (whichever first — count bounds memory, time bounds latency); the batch writes inside one transaction (EF SaveChanges = one round trip; bulk extensions for 10k+); only then are items removed/acked. Crash safety ladder: (0) accept loss (metrics — documented), (1) outbox table (same DB transaction as business write → relay publishes — exactly-once-ish), (2) durable broker (RabbitMQ/Kafka persistent + consumer acks), (3) write-ahead log for local buffers. Idempotency keys make retries safe (natural key or message id with unique constraint — duplicates become no-ops). Sizing: batch 100–1000 rows (parameter/lock sweet spot), flush interval 100ms–5s (latency vs efficiency), queue bound with drop/wait policy per data value. Ordering: single consumer preserves order; parallel consumers need partition keys (per-tenant ordering). Backpressure: bounded channel + Wait propagates slowness to producers instead of OOMing. Monitoring: queue depth, batch size histogram, write latency, dead-letter count. EF specifics: AddRange + SaveChanges (one round trip), ExecuteUpdate/Delete for set ops without loading, and transaction-per-batch (not per-row, not one giant).
internalWorking: AddRange tracks all entities then one SaveChanges emits batched INSERTs (EF batches by default up to provider limits). TransactionScope enlists the connection once. Channel drain loop parks with zero threads while idle; TryRead loop avoids per-item await overhead.
realWorldUsage: Telemetry ingestion, audit logs, outbox relays, import pipelines, and notification fan-out.
commonMistake: Per-row SaveChanges (N round trips — 100x slower), ack-before-commit (loss on crash), unbounded batches (giant transactions = locks + LOH), and no idempotency (retries duplicate).
technicalConversation: Ask what happens to in-flight batches on deploy/restart — outbox-or-accept-loss is a business decision, not an engineering detail.
interviewFollowUp: Why is ack-after-commit the critical ordering, and what breaks if you reverse it?
keyTakeaway: Batch by count-or-time, transact per batch, ack after commit, key idempotently. Size from latency and lock budgets.

questionText: What are the JSON serialization gotchas for dictionaries, sets, and special collections?
shortAnswer: System.Text.Json supports string-keyed dictionaries natively (non-string keys need converters or serialize as arrays); HashSet round-trips as arrays (order lost); polymorphism needs [JsonDerivedType]; cycles need ReferenceHandler.Preserve; case/naming policies must match both ends.
detailedAnswer: Dictionary<string, T> ↔ JSON object is native and fast. Non-string keys (int/Guid/enum Dictionary<int, X>) serialize as objects with stringified keys in STJ (Newtonsoft differs — arrays of KeyValuePair with setting) — cross-library contracts must be tested, and round-trip int keys carefully (string→int parse on read). HashSet<T>/SortedSet → JSON arrays; deserializing back works but ordering/dedup semantics are the receiver's problem. Polymorphic lists (List<Animal> with Cat/Dog) need [JsonPolymorphic]/[JsonDerivedType] discriminators or custom converters — otherwise base-only deserialization silently drops data. Cycles (parent↔children) throw by default — ReferenceHandler.Preserve adds $id/$ref metadata (payload shape changes — clients must handle it) or use DTOs to cut cycles (better). Naming: PropertyNamingPolicy.CamelCase + DictionaryKeyPolicy for keys; enum keys serialize via ToString (configure JsonStringEnumConverter consistently). Numbers: large longs beyond JS safe-integer lose precision (serialize as string). Records/required members: missing JSON members throw with required (validate contracts in tests with real payloads). Source-gen (JsonSerializerContext) demands all shapes known at compile time — dynamic/ExpandoObject breaks trimming/AOT (annotate or avoid).
internalWorking: STJ dictionary converter enumerates entries writing property names (string keys direct; others Convert.ToString with invariant culture); reading parses names back per key type. Preserve mode tracks object references in a dictionary ($id assignment, $ref emission) — allocation + payload overhead per object.
realWorldUsage: API contracts with maps/sets, config payloads, cached JSON blobs, event envelopes, and cross-service DTOs.
commonMistake: Assuming key types round-trip identically across libraries, polymorphic lists without discriminators (silent data loss), cycles crashing serializers (DTOs cut cycles), and camelCase mismatches between ends (contract tests with real JSON).
technicalConversation: Ask how they contract-test serialization — round-trip tests with real payloads plus schema snapshots catch the silent-loss class.
interviewFollowUp: Why do non-string dictionary keys create cross-library hazards, and how do you neutralize them?
keyTakeaway: String-keyed maps are native; everything else needs explicit policy + round-trip tests. DTOs cut cycles.

questionText: How do you implement sliding-window rate limiting with collections?
shortAnswer: Keep per-key timestamp queues (Queue<DateTime>): on each request, dequeue entries older than the window, then allow if count < limit. O(1) amortized per request, exact windows, bounded memory (≤ limit entries per key) — with eviction for idle keys.
detailedAnswer: Fixed windows (counter per minute) allow 2x bursts at boundaries; sliding-window log (timestamp queue) is exact: window = e.g. 60s, limit = 100. On request: while (q.Count > 0 && now - q.Peek() > window) q.Dequeue(); if (q.Count < limit) { q.Enqueue(now); allow } else reject (429 + Retry-After). Memory: ≤ limit timestamps per active key — bounded by design. Idle keys: sweep entries with empty/old queues periodically (or lazy-expire on access + background janitor) to avoid unbounded key growth (the real leak in this pattern). Concurrency: lock per key (fine-grained — stripe by key hash for hot keys) or ConcurrentQueue + lock the trim section; exactness under races needs the check-and-enqueue atomic (lock wins). Distributed: Redis sorted sets (ZADD/ZREMRANGEBYSCORE/ZCARD — same algorithm, shared) or token-bucket approximations. Alternatives: token bucket (bursty-friendly, less memory), leaky bucket (smooth output), fixed window with boundary-jitter acceptance (cheap, approximate). Headers: X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset + 429 Retry-After (client cooperation). Testing: fake clock (TimeProvider) for deterministic window tests — never Thread.Sleep in suites.
internalWorking: Each timestamp enqueued/dequeued once → O(1) amortized. Queue ring keeps memory at ≤ limit entries. Lock scope covers trim+check+enqueue (atomic decision); contention scales with per-key request rate (stripe hot keys).
realWorldUsage: API throttling, login-attempt limits, webhook delivery pacing, SMS/email send caps, and scraper protection.
commonMistake: Fixed-window boundary bursts (2x allowed), unbounded key growth (janitor missing), check-then-act races without lock (over-admit), and real clocks in tests (flaky suites — inject TimeProvider).
technicalConversation: Ask what happens at the window boundary under fixed windows — the 2x burst math (full quota at 00:59 + full at 01:00) motivates sliding windows.
interviewFollowUp: How would you scale this across 10 API replicas, and what exactness do you sacrifice?
keyTakeaway: Timestamp queues give exact sliding windows with bounded memory. Sweep idle keys; fake the clock in tests.

questionText: How do you pool reusable objects for hot paths without starving or leaking?
shortAnswer: Use ArrayPool<T>/MemoryPool<T> for buffers and ObjectPool<T> (Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool) for objects: rent → use → return in finally, cap pool size, never hold past scope, and measure before/after. Pools trade a little complexity for Gen0 silence.
detailedAnswer: ObjectPool<T> (DefaultObjectPoolProvider): var pool = provider.Create(new DefaultPooledObjectPolicy<Buffer>()); rent via pool.Get(), return via pool.Return(obj) — with policy Reset() clearing state (stale-state bugs live here: reset everything renter-visible). Size: DefaultObjectPool caps retained instances (MaximumRetained, default CPU-count*2 — overflow returns are dropped, not leaked). Rules mirror ArrayPool: return exactly once, in finally; don't hold (pool starvation = steady-state allocations return); don't share across owners ( torn state); reset on return (policy, not renter discipline). When pooling pays: per-request StringBuilder (the canonical sample), parsers, serializers, DTO mappers on hot endpoints — Gen0 drops visible in counters. When it doesn't: cold paths (complexity without benefit), tiny objects (pool overhead > alloc cost — sub-85ns allocs), or thread-static alternatives for single-threaded loops. Alternatives: ArrayPool (buffers), RecyclableMemoryStream (streams), ThreadLocal reuse (single-threaded), and struct-based designs (no heap at all). Diagnostics: pool exhaustion shows as allocation return (not errors); add rented/returned counters in debug builds. ASP.NET integrates ObjectPool via ObjectPoolProvider service (Razor reuses it for StringBuilder).
internalWorking: DefaultObjectPool keeps a thread-static fast slot + shared capped stack; Get is usually a field read, Return a write (near-free). Policies' Return(obj) returning false drops the instance (cap enforcement). StringBuilderPolicy resets Length/Capacity growth (caps runaway builders).
realWorldUsage: Hot-endpoint StringBuilders, log-message builders, parser scratch, serializer buffers, and middleware per-request state.
commonMistake: Forgetting Return (starvation), double Return (state corruption across renters), holding pooled objects in fields/caches (use-after-return), skipping Reset (data leaks between requests — a security issue for PII), and pooling cold paths (complexity theater).
technicalConversation: Ask what their hottest endpoint allocates per request — StringBuilder/buffer rentals with before/after Gen0 numbers is the standard optimization story.
interviewFollowUp: Why does the pool policy (not the renter) own Reset, and what security bug does that prevent?
keyTakeaway: Rent-use-return-finally, policy resets, capped retention. Pool hot paths only, measured.
